analysis.one_liner: Caps what hospitals can charge uninsured patients at the lowest price insurers pay.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its first day: it was referred to two House committees and a subcommittee, gained no cosponsors, and died there when the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: Uninsured patients are often billed a hospital's full, undiscounted
analysis.who_benefits: People without any health insurance who need hospital care. The bill would bar hospitals from billing them more than the lowest negotiated price the hospital accepts from any insurer or employer health plan, and would let the government penalize a hospital by the amount of the overcharge [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Hospitals could not hold an uninsured person liable for more than the lowest negotiated price they accept from any health insurer or group health plan for the same item or service [S2][S3].
A hospital that overcharged an uninsured patient above that lowest negotiated rate would owe a civil monetary penalty equal to the difference [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals and critical access hospitals, which would lose revenue from their highest-reimbursed patients and face penalties for overcharging the uninsured [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill only covers hospitals, not doctors' offices, clinics, or other providers, so an uninsured person could still face full undiscounted bills from other types of providers [S2][S3].
The bill does not reduce what insured patients owe or address the underlying prices themselves; it only extends the existing lowest insurer rate to the uninsured [S2][S3].
The bill never drew a single cosponsor, so there was no record of other lawmakers, industry groups, or patient groups weighing in on its design [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the roughly one in ten non-elderly Americans who go without insurance at some point each year, the bill would end the worst version of a common problem: being billed the hospital's top undiscounted rate for care an insurer would have paid a fraction of. The cost falls only on hospitals, which already give these rates to their biggest insurers. The honest limits are that it is a narrow fix (hospitals only) and never received enough attention to be tested, amended, or scored by any committee.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees on the day it was introduced, then to the Health Subcommittee, and neither committee ever considered it before the Congress ended [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Chris Collins of New York introduced the bill on June 20, 2019 [S1].
It was referred that day to the Energy and Commerce Committee and to the Ways and Means Committee [S1][S5].
The next day, it was referred to the Health Subcommittee of Energy and Commerce [S5].
No further action was taken; the bill never received a hearing or a vote, and expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S1][S5].
The bill had no cosponsors at any point [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals, which avoided a rule capping what they can bill uninsured patients at insurer rates, plus the two House committees, which kept discretion over whether to act on hospital billing legislation at all.

for.name: Rep. Chris Collins (R-NY)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and put it before the House, though he recruited no cosponsors [S1][S4].

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on June 20, 2019 and sent it to its Health Subcommittee the next day, then took no further action for the rest of the Congress [S5].

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on June 20, 2019 and took no action on the bill [S5].

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor and no cosponsors from either party, so no partisan pattern on the merits ever formed [S4].

industries.note: Hospitals routinely bill uninsured patients at full list price, several times what insurers pay, and this bill would cap those bills at the insurer's lowest negotiated rate plus penalties for overcharging. Hospitals' interest in the bill ran against uninsured patients', and it never became law.

industries.industry: Health insurers and employer health plans
industries.note: The bill defines the cap as the rates hospitals already negotiate with insurers, effectively making the insurer-negotiated price the benchmark of fair pricing for the uninsured. Insurers neither pay nor gain much, but their negotiated rates become the reference point for everyone.
